title: Direct Democracy
objective: After this level you can explain government where citizens vote on everything themselves.
summary: In direct democracy citizens decide issues themselves, as in the Swiss Landsgemeinde and New England town meetings. Large states make it hard, so it mostly works inside representative systems.

cards.headline: Once a year, voters in two Swiss cantons make their laws by raising a hand.
cards.body: In the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden, voters gather in the open air for the Landsgemeinde and vote on laws and taxes by a show of hands. No representatives in between. Just you, your neighbors and your right arm.

cards.headline: Cutting out the middle
cards.body: That's direct democracy: citizens make the decisions themselves instead of electing officials to decide for them. Britannica puts the contrast simply. In a representative democracy you vote for people; in a direct democracy you often vote on the issue itself. It's the closest thing to Level 7's Rousseau in practice: laws people make together, for themselves.

cards.fact: New England towns govern themselves the same way.
cards.context: A town meeting is an assembly of a town's qualified voters. Together they elect officials and school boards, and debate and vote on taxes and spending. Imagine your town's budget decided not by a council but by whoever turns up, one hand at a time.

cards.headline: The catch: size
cards.body: So why doesn't every country work this way? Britannica notes the long-standing argument that direct democracy can't work across the space and time of large modern states. Picture a whole country trying to fit into one town square. Today it mostly lives inside representative systems, as specific tools rather than the whole machine. And the square has another price: critics complain a secret ballot is impossible when everyone can see your hand.

learned: Direct democracy: citizens decide issues themselves

questions.prompt: How do voters decide at the Landsgemeinde in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden?

options.label: By electing a parliament to decide for them
options.rationale: The point of the Landsgemeinde is deciding in person.

options.label: By mailing in a secret ballot
options.rationale: Voting is open, by raised hands.

options.label: By a show of hands at an open-air assembly
By letting the cantonal council vote in private
options.rationale: Voters decide themselves, in the open.

questions.explanation: Once a year, voters gather in the open air and vote on laws and taxes by a show of hands.

questions.prompt: Why does direct democracy today mostly work inside representative systems?

options.label: It is hard to run across the scale of a large modern state
Citizens are not allowed to vote on issues anywhere
options.rationale: Glarus shows they can, on a small scale.

options.label: It was abolished everywhere in the 1800s
options.rationale: The Landsgemeinde and town meetings still run.

options.label: Representatives are required by every constitution
options.rationale: The limit given is size, not a universal rule.

questions.explanation: Britannica notes the argument that direct democracy can't work across the space and time of large modern states, so today it mostly works as specific tools.

questions.prompt: Direct democracy: which Level 7 thinker argued that legitimate laws come from people agreeing together on laws for the common good?

options.label: Thomas Hobbes
options.rationale: Hobbes had people hand their freedom to an all-powerful sovereign.

options.label: John Locke
options.rationale: Locke stressed natural rights and consent, not the general will.

options.label: Max Weber
options.rationale: Weber defined power, authority and the state.

questions.explanation: Rousseau's general will: people agree together to live by laws aimed at the common good, laws they make for themselves.
